blocks.html:
“We already do a planning retreat every January,” the owner says. “How is this different?”

You have about twenty seconds. What most people say next is a description of the product — workshops, a plan, software, quarterly meetings — and the owner hears the retreat they already pay for, with more steps.

What they're actually asking is narrower and more useful: will this change anything? The answer that lands isn't a feature list. It's that the firm does two things, and the second one is the reason the first one survives contact with a busy Tuesday.

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to:

  1. Explain the practice in two sentences, without product jargon or a price.
  2. Separate the plan from the operating system in your own words, and say why one without the other fails.
  3. Place the practice against what an owner has already tried — a retreat, a binder, a consultant's report.

About 15 minutes, including one short video. This course is the overview: it's for talking about OASYS and recommending it to the right prospect. Mastering OASYS is the implementer training.

blocks.html:
What changed since these videos were recorded (2026)
Practice lead is Jesse Kreun (acting Managing Principal). Every engagement starts with some form of fact-finding assessment, but it is not always a full CSP. A CSP usually recommends OASYS, and OASYS can begin without one.

Words you'll hear. CSP — Client Success Plan, our full fact-finding assessment. SPE — Strategic Planning and Execution, the older name for this practice. BOS — Business Operating System: the way a company leads and manages day to day. KPI — key performance indicator, a number that shows whether something is on track. Rocks — the few priorities the leadership team commits to for the next 90 days.

The same question, two answers

An owner asks what you do. Both answers below are true. Watch where each conversation goes.

The product answerThe practice answer
What you say“We run a two-day planning session, agree goals for the year, and then meet weekly and quarterly on a platform called ninety.io.”“We do two things. We build the plan — where you're going and how you'll get there. Then we fix the way the company actually runs week to week, so the plan doesn't die in February.”
What the owner hears“That's my January retreat, plus software and more meetings.”“The plan I already write might actually happen this time.”
Where it goesThey compare you to the facilitator they already use, on price and days.They ask how it works — which is the conversation you want.

The difference isn't confidence. It's that the second answer names a problem the owner already has: a plan they can't execute. Almost every owner has one. Very few have an operating system that carries it.

Two jobs, one practice

A strategic plan is the bedrock of lasting growth. But a plan alone changes nothing, so the practice does two jobs:

  • Builds the strategic plan — a clear picture of where the company is going and how it will get there.
  • Upgrades the Business Operating System (BOS) — the way the company actually leads and manages day to day, so the plan gets executed.

OASYS is OneAccord's BOS. ninety.io is the software platform it runs on. One is the way the company operates; the other is where that way of operating is kept visible and consistent.

A note on names. Older materials and Doug's videos call this practice SPE (Strategic Planning and Execution), and you'll sometimes hear “Oasis.” Today it's the OASYS Strategic Planning service line. Same thing.

Who it's for

Owner-led businesses from $10M in revenue upward, with no upper cap — the firm's sweet spot is roughly $25M to $100M. The practice operates at the leadership level: you're hired by the CEO and you work with the leadership team, not with the whole company and not around the CEO.

The signal that an owner is ready isn't size. It's that at least one of their three objectives has become a real problem: achieving the purpose and goals they set out for, time freedom (a company that runs without them in every decision), or enterprise value and the options that come with it. An owner comfortable on all three has no reason to buy.

What to take from Doug's introduction

  • Deep operator experience: nearly 50 years in business, including senior roles in the PC and barcoding/RFID industries, before moving into coaching small and mid-sized businesses in 2012.
  • Operating systems are the specialty: after reading Traction he became the first EOS-certified implementer in Washington State (2017), later worked with Pinnacle Business Guides and Scaling Up, and now takes an independent, best-of-breed approach.
  • The coaching mindset: you don't run to the base of Mount Rainier and start climbing. You prepare, gather tools, learn the disciplines — then the leadership team climbs its own mountain, with a coach alongside.

How it starts, and how it doesn't

Every engagement begins with some form of fact-finding assessment — but not always a full CSP. A CSP usually recommends OASYS, and OASYS can begin without one. The assessment is how you learn enough to be useful; it isn't a toll gate.

What you never do in an overview conversation: quote a price, promise a timeline you haven't scoped, or describe the engagement as a set of workshops without the operating-system half. Price and scope belong with the Managing Principal. Your job here is to explain and to recognise the right prospect — not to sell a package.

blocks.prompt: What are the two things the OASYS Strategic Planning practice does for a client?
options: Writes a business plan and finds investors
Builds a strategic plan and upgrades the client's Business Operating System so the plan gets executed
Replaces the leadership team and runs operations
Installs ninety.io and trains staff on the software
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. A plan, plus the operating system that makes it happen.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: The practice builds the strategic plan and upgrades the BOS so the plan is actually executed. Software installation alone is neither half.

blocks.prompt: How do OASYS and ninety.io relate?
options: They're competing systems; clients pick one
ninety.io is OneAccord's consulting brand; OASYS is the software
OASYS is OneAccord's Business Operating System; ninety.io is the software platform it runs on
ninety.io is only used for scheduling meetings
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Exactly. OASYS is the system; ninety.io is where the client runs it.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: OASYS is the system — the principles and practices. ninety.io is the platform that keeps it consistent.

blocks.prompt: In Doug's Mount Rainier metaphor, what does good coaching look like?
options: Getting to the summit as fast as possible
Doing the climb for the client
Preparing first — tools and disciplines — then the team climbs its own mountain
Skipping preparation because experienced teams don't need it
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. Preparation and discipline first, then the team climbs its own mountain.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: The point is preparation: tools and disciplines first, then the team climbs with a coach alongside.

Write what you'd say, in your own words — the way you'd actually say it out loud.

blocks.promptHtml:
Different conditions: the prospect has already decided what they want.

A fellow principal introduces you to the CEO of a $40M manufacturer. She says: “We know what our strategy is. What we need is someone to run the plan with our team — the annual session and the quarterly reviews. We don't need the software, and we don't need a consultant living in our business.”

What do you say, and what do you do next?
rubric: Recognises what she's actually describing — the operating-system half of the practice — and says so, rather than arguing she needs a plan
Explains why the two halves are usually done together: the plan survives because the way the company runs week to week carries it
Asks what's happened with previous plans before proposing anything, because the answer decides the shape of the engagement
Does not quote a price or promise a scope, and routes any scoping or pricing question to the Managing Principal
Leaves with a concrete next step that respects her position — an assessment or a conversation with the Managing Principal — rather than a pitch
blocks.coachContext: This prospect is asking for the operating-system half and calling it 'running the plan'. The practice is plan plus BOS; the reason is that a plan without a way of operating doesn't survive the quarter. The useful move is to ask what happened to previous plans — many owners have a binder nobody opened, which is the diagnosis. Scope and pricing are the Managing Principal's, never quoted in conversation. Every engagement starts with some form of fact-finding assessment, not always a full CSP. No prices.

blocks.instructions:
Open the OASYS Strategic Planning page on oneaccord.co and read it the way a prospect would:
  • The headline — what does it promise, in the owner's language?
  • The problems it names — pick the one that sounds most like an owner you actually know.
  • The gap — what does the page not say that you'd have to explain in person?

That last one is the part of your two-sentence answer that the page can't do for you.
